title: Supreme Court Upholds Birthright Citizenship; GOP Lawmakers Push Legislative Workaround
excerpt: The 6-3 ruling struck down Trump's executive order, but Republican senators are now introducing bills to restrict citizenship for children of undocumented immigrants and temporary visa holders through federal law.
body:
• The Supreme Court ruled 6-3 in Trump v. Barbara that children born in the U.S. to parents unlawfully or temporarily present are citizens under the 14th Amendment, striking down Trump's executive order.
  • Sen. Eric Schmitt (R-Mo.) introduced the American Citizenship Act; Sen. Jim Banks (R-Ind.) followed with the Citizenship Act of 2026 using "invaders" language to limit birthright citizenship through federal law.
  • Justice Kavanaugh's concurrence — finding the order conflicted with statute, not the Constitution — has become the legal roadmap for the GOP's legislative push.
  • The ruling protects U.S.-born children of nearly 300,000 Indian H-1B visa holders and over 1.2 million in the employment-based green card backlog.

The Supreme Court's 6-3 decision in Trump v. Barbara on June 30 should have settled the matter: children born on American soil to parents who are unlawfully or temporarily in the United States are citizens at birth under the 14th Amendment. Chief Justice John Roberts, writing for the majority, grounded the opinion in the 1898 United States v. Wong Kim Ark precedent.

"Citizenship, then and now, was the right to have rights — to freely participate in our political community. The Framers of the Fourteenth Amendment extended that promise to 'every free-born person in this land.' We keep that promise today."

— Chief Justice John Roberts, majority opinion in Trump v. Barbara

But within two weeks, Republican lawmakers moved to do through Congress what the Court blocked from the executive branch.

The Legislative Push

On July 14, Sen. Eric Schmitt (R-Mo.) introduced the American Citizenship Act, which would limit automatic birthright citizenship to children of U.S. citizens and lawful permanent residents. The next day, Sen. Jim Banks (R-Ind.) filed the Citizenship Act of 2026, declaring that "any person who enters the United States without authorization or for the purpose of engaging in birth tourism is considered an invader" and amending the Immigration and Nationality Act to exclude their children from birthright citizenship, according to USA Today.

"Wong Kim Ark</em> precedent.</p> <blockquote class="pull-quote"><p>"Citizenship, then and now, was the right to have rights — to freely participate in our political community."

"Wong Kim Ark</em> precedent.</p> <blockquote class="pull-quote"><p>"Citizenship, then and now, was the right to have rights — to freely participate in our political community."

Banks' bill would require mothers to hold legal immigration status for their U.S.-born children to receive citizenship, with additional restrictions related to fathers and surrogacy, according to IndyStar. Rep. John McGuire III (R-Va.) introduced a parallel measure in the House.

Kavanaugh's Roadmap

The legislative strategy draws from Justice Brett Kavanaugh's concurrence in Barbara. While Kavanaugh voted to strike down the executive order, he did so on narrower grounds — finding it conflicted with an existing federal statute rather than the 14th Amendment itself. He suggested Congress is the proper institution to define exceptions to birthright citizenship, provided they are "relevantly similar" to those recognized in Wong Kim Ark: children of diplomats, enemy forces, or occupying armies.

Banks' bill tries to exploit this opening by classifying unauthorized immigration as an "invasion" and arguing that children born to people in violation of immigration law fall under Wong Kim Ark's exception for those not "bound to render obedience" to the U.S. government.

Constitutional Barriers Remain

Both bills face steep odds. The majority opinion explicitly rejected the argument that parental immigration status determines birthright citizenship — a constitutional holding that any statute would need to survive. The Court stated that changes to citizenship requirements would require a constitutional amendment.

"I will be asking for a Rehearing by the United States Supreme Court, IMMEDIATELY. This miscarriage of justice will destroy America if they don't change their absolutely insane decision."

— President Donald Trump, via Truth Social

Rehearing requests are rarely granted and require a majority of justices to agree — a remote prospect given the decisive 6-3 margin.

What It Means for the Indian Diaspora

For nearly 300,000 Indian H-1B visa holders and the more than 1.2 million individuals in the employment-based green card backlog — many facing decades-long waits for permanent residency — the ruling provides concrete reassurance that their U.S.-born children's citizenship is constitutionally protected.

Chinten Patel, executive director of Indian American Impact, said: "Today the Supreme Court looked at those families and said: 'Your children are American. They belong here.'" Rep. Pramila Jayapal added: "Our Constitution does not have asterisks. It does not have exceptions for who deserves to belong," according to India West.

The proposed legislation could reclassify children of temporary visa holders — including H-1B, L-1, and student visa categories — as outside birthright citizenship protections. Immigration attorneys say such a statute would face immediate constitutional challenge. With Schmitt's and Banks' bills in the Senate and the House Freedom Caucus pushing for H.R. 2, the Secure the Border Act, birthright citizenship will remain a live issue through the 2026 midterms — even as the legal path to restrict it stays narrow.
